nameStory: The post oak earned its name from early settlers who discovered its wood was perfect for making fence posts. The tree's dense, rot-resistant timber could withstand decades in the ground without decay, making it invaluable for building property boundaries across the frontier.
description: Post oak is a medium-sized deciduous tree that typically grows 30-50 feet tall with a rounded, spreading crown. It's a tough survivor that thrives in poor, dry soils where other oaks struggle. The tree is easily recognized by its distinctive cross-shaped leaves that look almost like a child's drawing of a tree leaf, with rounded lobes that form a cross pattern. It's a member of the white oak group, producing sweet acorns that wildlife love.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The most distinctive feature - leaves form a clear cross shape with 3-5 rounded lobes arranged like a cruciform pattern. The undersides feel fuzzy and soft to the touch, covered in fine hairs that give them a whitish appearance.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark is light gray to brown with deep furrows and ridges, feeling rough and chunky under your fingers. On younger branches, the bark is smoother with a grayish color.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a broad, rounded crown with sturdy, often twisted branches. The tree has a stocky, rugged appearance and grows slowly, often developing a gnarled character in harsh sites.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Acorns are small, oval-shaped, and sit in shallow caps that cover about one-third of the nut. They're sweet-tasting (though not recommended for humans) and fall in autumn.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are small, rounded, and reddish-brown, clustered at branch tips. They feel smooth and have a slightly resinous texture when fresh.

habitat: In New England, post oak grows at the northern edge of its range, preferring dry, sandy or rocky soils on hilltops, ridge tops, and south-facing slopes. You'll find it in areas with poor soil drainage where other trees struggle, often mixed with other drought-tolerant species like bear oak and pitch pine.

seasonality.spring: Small yellowish-green flowers appear in May as leaves emerge. New leaves unfold with a soft, fuzzy texture and pale green color.
seasonality.summer: Leaves mature to dark green above while maintaining their fuzzy white undersides. The distinctive cross-shaped leaf pattern is most obvious during full summer foliage.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow-brown to russet, and acorns ripen and fall. Fall color is usually not spectacular, ranging from yellow to brown.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the tree's sturdy, often twisted architecture. Small clustered buds at branch tips and persistent acorn caps help with identification.

funFact: Post oak wood is so incredibly rot-resistant that fence posts made from it can last over 100 years in the ground - some pioneers' original post oak fences are still standing today after more than a century!
confusionNotes: Post oak's cross-shaped leaves make it fairly distinctive, but it can be confused with white oak, which has more deeply lobed leaves with pointed rather than rounded lobes. Remember: post oak leaves look like a cross, white oak leaves look like they have fingers reaching out.
contextualKnowledge: Post oak is much more common in the southern United States, where it forms vast forests. In New England, you're seeing trees at the very northern limit of their range, making each sighting special. These northern populations are often smaller and more gnarled than their southern cousins.
compareHints: Among New England oaks, post oak is unique for its cross-shaped leaves with rounded lobes and fuzzy undersides. White oak has more deeply cut leaves with pointed lobes, while bear oak is much smaller and shrubbier. The combination of the cross-leaf pattern and hairy leaf undersides makes post oak unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England oaks, white oak is distinguished by its evenly rounded leaf lobes without bristle tips (unlike red oak group species) and its light gray bark.

Among New England's oaks, northern red oak is distinguished by its pointed leaf lobes (white oak has rounded lobes), its large size (much bigger than bear oak or dwarf chinkapin oak), and its relatively shallow acorn caps (deeper than scarlet oak, shallower than pin oak).
Bear oak stands apart from other New England oaks by being consistently shrubby rather than tree-like, even at maturity.
Among the red oak group, black oak has the deepest leaf lobes - much deeper than red oak or pin oak.
Unlike white oak with its deeply rounded lobes, chestnut oak has scalloped edges with rounded teeth.
Among New England's white oak group, swamp white oak is unique in its preference for wet areas and its distinctive leaf shape with deeper bottom lobes.
Among New England's red oaks, scarlet oak stands out with its deeply dissected leaves that have the most pronounced sinuses (indentations).
Unlike other New England oaks that have lobed leaves (deeply indented edges), dwarf chinkapin oak has simple leaves with rounded teeth like a saw blade.
English oak stands out among New England's oaks by having the leaf and acorn stems completely reversed from most natives - very short leaf stems but very long acorn stems.
Among New England oaks, pin oak stands out for its combination of deeply-cut leaves with sharp points and its distinctive pin-like branching pattern.
Among New England oaks, bur oak is easily distinguished by its enormous acorns with fringed caps and extremely deeply-lobed leaves.
Unlike most New England oaks, chinkapin oak has toothed rather than lobed leaves, setting it apart immediately from white oak, red oak, and others.
Unlike our native oaks, Turkey oak has those telltale bristly buds and bristle-tipped leaves that you can actually feel.
Sawtooth oak is completely different from all other New England oaks because of its simple, toothed leaves rather than the lobed leaves found on species like white oak, red oak, or black oak.
Among New England oaks, willow oak is unmistakable due to its unlobed, willow-like leaves - all other regional oaks have distinctly lobed or toothed leaves.
Among New England oaks, shingle oak is instantly recognizable by its simple, unlobed leaves - all other common oaks in the region have the typical lobed leaves we associate with oaks.
